answer_text:
Let

\[
Q=\sum_{i=1}^n a_i^2,\qquad P=\sum_{1\le i<j\le n}a_i a_j.
\]

We want the largest constant \(C\) such that

\[
Q\ge C P
\]

for all \(a_i\ge 0\).

Assume \(n\ge 2\). We use the identity

\[
\left(\sum_{i=1}^n a_i\right)^2
=
\sum_{i=1}^n a_i^2+2\sum_{i<j}a_i a_j
=
Q+2P.
\]

By Cauchy–Schwarz,

\[
\left(\sum_{i=1}^n a_i\right)^2
\le n\sum_{i=1}^n a_i^2
=
nQ.
\]

Therefore,

\[
Q+2P\le nQ,
\]

so

\[
2P\le (n-1)Q,
\]

and hence

\[
Q\ge \frac{2}{n-1}P.
\]

Thus \(C=\frac{2}{n-1}\) always works.

To show that no larger constant can work, take

\[
a_1=a_2=\cdots=a_n=1.
\]

Then

\[
Q=n,\qquad P=\binom{n}{2}=\frac{n(n-1)}2.
\]

The inequality becomes

\[
n\ge C\cdot \frac{n(n-1)}2,
\]

so necessarily

\[
C\le \frac{2}{n-1}.
\]

Therefore, for \(n\ge 2\), the largest possible constant is

\[
\boxed{\frac{2}{n-1}}.
\]

If \(n=1\), the sum over \(i<j\) is empty, so the inequality is \(a_1^2\ge 0\), which holds for every constant \(C\); in that degenerate case there is no largest finite constant.
